transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me, I really appreciate it. Um, I hope I'm not wasting your time—it's probably just a little quirk, really. But, well, I guess what brought me in is that I've been having a bit of trouble just... staying in my chair? 

Like, during staff meetings at the school where I teach, or even just sitting down for dinner, I'll suddenly get up when everyone else is seated. I always try to make myself useful, you know, like I'll pop up to refill the coffee, or go check on a handout, or just walk to the back of the room. But I guess I do it even when nothing is really urgent. My family sort of gently pointed it out, so I thought I should ask a professional about it. 

Is that... is that the sort of thing you can help with? I just want to make sure I'm in the right place and explaining it okay.

When you're sitting down and feel the urge to get up, does it feel more like your body just can't stay still and needs to move, or does it feel more like you're anxious or uncomfortable and getting up helps calm you down?

Oh, um... I don't think it's anxiety. I really hope I don't come across as a nervous person! I think it's more just... my body just sort of expects to be doing something? If that makes sense? 

It's like I just have this momentum. Especially lately. Since the house got a lot quieter after my youngest left for college, I just... I keep busy. I'll move straight from lesson planning to throwing in a load of laundry, then I'm off to help with softball practice, and then I'm chopping food for a community event... just without much of a pause at all. 

I always tell myself it's just being productive and helpful, you know? But even on nights when I promised myself I would finally just sit down and rest... I just keep going. I just don't seem to stop. Is it okay that I'm explaining it like this? I just want to make sure I'm answering your question properly.
Have you always been someone who needs to stay busy and active like this, even going back to when you were a child or teenager? Or is this something that's gotten noticeably worse recently?

Well, um... I suppose I've always been a bit of a busy bee, really. I hope that's alright to say. My mother, bless her, she used to joke that I wore a path right into the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old. I just liked to make sure my pencils were perfectly sharp, you know? 

And, um, I think my teachers back then... well, they were very kind, but my report cards usually said I was bright—which was nice of them to say!—but that I maybe had a little trouble staying in my seat or waiting my turn to speak. I was just so eager to participate, I think. 

So it's not entirely new, no. It's just... maybe it stands out a bit more now that I don't have the kids at home to chase after. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not overcomplicating things.

When you're going through these busy periods where you're constantly moving from one thing to another, how many hours of sleep are you actually getting at night? And do you feel rested, or do you feel like you need more sleep?

Oh, sleep... well, I sleep just fine, I think! I hope I didn't give the impression that I'm up all night. I really try to get a good night's rest, usually about six or seven hours, which I think is pretty normal for someone my age? 

I mean, sometimes I might wake up a little early and just decide to start the day, maybe get a head start on grading papers or something, but I don't feel exhausted or anything. I actually feel quite rested. I certainly don't feel like I'm running on empty. 

I just... I like to make the most of my day, you know? Is six or seven hours alright? I hope that doesn't sound like I'm neglecting my health.

When you're in these periods of being very busy and active, do you notice your mood feels different—like are you feeling unusually happy, energized, or like everything is going great? Or does your mood stay pretty much the same as usual?

Oh, um... no, I don't think my mood changes much at all. I'm just... well, I'm just me! I really hope I haven't made it sound like I'm, you know, overly emotional or bouncing off the walls with excitement or anything. 

I don't feel unusually happy or like everything is perfect... just, normal, I suppose? I try very hard to keep an even keel, especially since I feel like I need to be a steady presence for my students. So, my mood stays pretty much the same, even when I'm rushing around. 

Is that what you were asking? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information. I hope I'm explaining things clearly enough!
When you're in conversations or meetings, do you find yourself interrupting others or blurting things out before they've finished speaking? Or do you tend to think before you speak?

Oh, well... I do try my very best to be polite, I really do. But, um... sometimes I suppose I might get just a little bit ahead of myself? I hope that doesn't make me sound rude. 

It's just that, especially in group discussions—like at my book club or during our curriculum meetings at school—someone will be talking, and the response just sort of... forms in my head so quickly. And before I can even remind myself to wait, I've already jumped in and blurted it out. 

I don't mean to cut anyone off, I promise! I just get so engaged in the conversation, and I want to contribute, and it just slips out before they've quite finished their thought. I always feel a bit terribly about it afterward. Is that... is that the sort of thing you mean? I hope you don't think I'm a terrible listener.

You mentioned feeling a bit terribly about interrupting people at book club and your curriculum meetings. Has this habit of interrupting or blurting things out caused any real problems for you—like affecting your relationships with colleagues or friends, or impacting how people perceive you professionally?

Oh, well... I wouldn't say they are *real* problems, exactly. I mean, I certainly hope they don't think badly of me! But... I suppose, if I'm being completely honest with you—and I do want to make sure I'm giving you all the right information—it has started to affect my relationships just a little bit. At work, and in my community. 

I've started to notice that people... well, they seem to lose patience with me sometimes during our curriculum meetings and at book club. I can see it in their faces or when they sigh after I've jumped in too quickly. And instead of enjoying the discussion and feeling connected to everyone, I just end up leaving feeling terribly embarrassed about it all. 

I really do try my best to be a good colleague and a good friend, I promise. Does that make sense? I just hope I haven't completely ruined their impression of me. Do you think that's something I can fix if I just try a little harder to be quiet?

You mentioned feeling embarrassed about interrupting people, and noticing that colleagues and friends seem to lose patience with you. On a scale where 1 is 'barely bothers me' and 10 is 'seriously affecting my life,' how much are all of these symptoms—the difficulty sitting still, the constant activity, and the interrupting—actually interfering with your ability to do your job well or maintain close relationships?

Oh, a number... goodness, I want to give you the right answer. I really hope I'm not making a mountain out of a molehill, but... maybe a 3? Or a 4? 

I mean, I still do my job, and I care so much about my students. But... well, like I said, it has started to affect my relationships at work and in my community. It’s just that people lose patience with me in our curriculum meetings and at book club. And instead of feeling connected to everyone, which is what I really want, I just leave feeling so embarrassed. 

I don't want you to think my whole life is falling apart or that I'm completely incapable! It's just a mild bump in the road, really. I just want to get back to being a good colleague and friend. Does a 3 or a 4 sound reasonable to you? I hope I'm not overstating it... I just want to be as helpful as possible for you.

When you're trying to focus on one task—like grading papers or reading a book—do you find it hard to concentrate, or do you find your mind wandering to other things? Or is it mainly just that your body won't stay still, but your attention is actually pretty good?

Oh, well... goodness, I think my attention is actually quite good! I really do. I mean, as a teacher, you simply have to be able to focus, don't you? 

When I'm grading papers or reading for my book club, I... well, I don't think my mind wanders terribly much. I try very hard to stay on task. It's really more of a... a physical restlessness, I suppose? Like my body just wants to be doing something, even if my brain is perfectly happy looking at an essay. 

I mean, I might tap my foot, or I might need to get up and pace for just a moment, but I'm still thinking about the work! I promise I'm not daydreaming or losing my train of thought. I really do pride myself on being thorough. 

Is that... is that normal? I hope it doesn't sound like I'm neglecting my duties. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of things. I think my concentration is mostly fine, really. Does that make sense?

You mentioned your concentration is mostly fine when you're grading or reading. But in your daily life—like when you're planning lessons or trying to organize your thoughts before a meeting—do you find yourself having trouble keeping your attention on one thing, or do you lose track of what you were trying to do?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say that happens. I really try to be very organized, especially with lesson planning. It's so important for the students, you know? 

I... well, I don't think I lose track of what I'm doing. I mean, I might jump up to grab a different pen, or maybe I'll sort through some papers while I'm thinking, but my mind is still very much on the lesson. I don't find my attention slipping away or anything like that. I really do try to stay right on top of things. 

I hope that's the right kind of answer? I just don't want you to think I'm scattered or not doing a good job preparing for my classes. I think I keep my thoughts together quite well, actually. Is that what you were looking for?

When you're teaching a class or leading a discussion with your students, do you ever find it difficult to stay focused on what one student is saying, or do you sometimes miss details because your attention shifts to something else in the room?

Oh, goodness, no. I really don't think I do that. When my students are speaking, I am fully engaged with them. They're my priority, after all! 

I mean, I might be... you know, walking around the classroom while they talk, or maybe adjusting the blinds if the sun is in someone's eyes, but I am absolutely listening to every word they say. I don't miss details. I would feel just awful if a student thought I wasn't paying attention to them. 

I pride myself on being very present for them. I hope that doesn't sound boastful! I just... I want to assure you that my classroom is a very supportive environment. I'm doing okay in that regard, aren't I? I really hope I'm giving you the information you need.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a longstanding pattern of physical restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, constant need for activity, and impulsivity (interrupting/blurting out) that began in childhood and persists into adulthood. While she denies significant inattention and reports good concentration, the core symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity are clearly present and causing mild-to-moderate functional impairment in social and occupational domains. The symptom profile, lifelong history, and documented impact on relationships and workplace interactions are consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type (F90.1) or Combined Type (F90.2); however, given the absence of documented inattention symptoms and the predominance of hyperactivity-impulsivity, F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) is assigned to reflect the clinical presentation without overspecifying the subtype.
